summary: Round 2, production. F1-F9 verified fixed. F1: the only CommitLog reads left in CheckpointWriter are log.epoch() on the constructing thread and log.nextSequence()/log.offsets() inside capture(), reached only from the synchronized observe() on the commit thread; writeIfDirty is synchronized on the same monitor and reads only pendingSequence/pendingStreams, so the ticker touches CommitLog not at all. F2: on IOException the counter is reset and the dirty flag left set, so the retry is bounded at one PUT per T plus one per K deltas; the tick loop always blocks on awaitNextTick, so no hot loop. Request rate re-checked end to end: one PUT per trigger regardless of stream or pod count, no LIST or GET added, and an idle (non-dirty) cluster issues zero requests -- the rate scales with deltas/K and seconds/T and with nothing forbidden. F8: putIfAbsent's silent lost race is behaviourally right (the retry-after-a-failed-PUT-that-landed case converges in one tick with a byte-identical body), though the stated reason for it is impossible and the empty Optional is discarded -- see F13. F9: the rewritten cost claim checks out against the sources -- requirements.md line 30 is 'zero object-store requests from consumers', and M4/SPEC.md line 372 is 'Checkpoints cost one PUT per K deltas or T seconds -- negligible'. F10 unchanged in my view: it is M4.8c/M4.9's. The SPEC already owns it at lines 266 and 279 ('the whole ckpt/ prefix, which grows with uptime because nothing deletes checkpoints until M7' / 'recovery must find the newest checkpoint without a list'), and this commit's contribution to the existing recovery LIST is one extra key per K deltas -- a 1/K factor on a dimension that already exists, not a new one. Five minors, all cheap, none corrupting.

findings.title: F4 applied to writeIfDirty but not to awaitNextTick, which it also named
findings.failure_scenario: tickForever wraps only `if (!closed) writeOnTick();` in catch (Throwable). `ticker.awaitNextTick()` sits in its own try that catches InterruptedException alone, so an unchecked throw from a Ticker escapes the while loop and terminates the ckpt-tick virtual thread with nothing logged -- the exact silent, permanent death F4 described, and below K deltas per period the T trigger is all there is. The shipped ticker is Thread.sleep(interval) with an interval checkPolicy has already forced positive, so production cannot reach it today; the seam is package-private and M4.9 is expected to retune T through it. Remedy is a statement move, not new prose: put the whole loop body inside the existing try, or wrap the while.

findings.title: The putIfAbsent justification is impossible, and the one anomaly it could report is dropped
findings.failure_scenario: The javadoc says an unconditional put 'lets a leader that does not yet know it is fenced overwrite its successor's checkpoint at the same key', and the backlog row repeats it. It cannot happen: `keys` is `new LogKeys(prefix, log.epoch())` and LogKeys.checkpointKeyFor embeds the epoch via logPrefix(), so a fenced leader at epoch E and its successor at E+1 write under different prefixes and can never collide at one key. putIfAbsent is still right -- M4/SPEC.md line 196 names it for 'the delta chain, the seal and checkpoints' -- but the recorded reason is false, and this row's own history is a list of false justifications caught in review. Two consequences worth stating instead: (a) the lost race is safe here for a reason worth writing down, namely that the only way to reach an occupied key is this writer retrying a PUT that reported IOException but landed, where the body is byte-identical because pods and pendingStreams cannot move without pendingSequence moving too; and (b) because no second writer should exist at this epoch, an empty Optional that is NOT such a retry is in-band evidence of two live leaders on one epoch -- the I1 condition -- and it is discarded without so much as a log line.

findings.title: capture() assigns pendingSequence before pendingStreams, latching the fatal skew direction if it throws between them
findings.failure_scenario: capture() sets pendingSequence = log.nextSequence(), then builds the streams map, then assigns pendingStreams. observe() now swallows Throwable, so a throw between those two statements (realistically an OutOfMemoryError while copying a large offsets map -- log.offsets() is Map.copyOf and the loop allocates a StreamOffsets per stream) leaves pendingSequence newer than pendingStreams and the process alive. dirty is not set on that path, but it may already be set from an earlier commit whose write has not happened yet, in which case the next T tick writes a checkpoint whose sequence is N and whose offsets predate N -- M4.9 then resumes at N with delta N-1's offsets missing and every stream in it rewinds. That is the same I2 the F1 fix exists to remove, arriving through the F3 fix's door. Remedy is a one-line reorder with no new comment: build `streams` first, assign pendingStreams and pendingSequence adjacently at the end.

findings.title: checkPolicy moved ahead of tryAcquire, but the identical lease-held-forever window remains one argument over
findings.failure_scenario: The 7-arg start does Objects.requireNonNull(ticker) for the renew ticker but not for checkpointTicker. A caller passing a null checkpointTicker acquires the lease, seals the predecessor, recovers and opens the chain, then takes an NPE out of the CheckpointWriter constructor -- past `catch (IOException)`, with the lease held and the renewer thread already renewing it. That is F6's failure verbatim, and F6's remedy hoisted only the K/T check. More generally the window is not specific to the writer: every call between leases.tryAcquire() and the return -- firstInheritableAncestor, recoverChainEnd, seal, recover, open, Thread.start -- can throw unchecked and leak the term the same way, which is pre-existing and is why this is not raised higher. The cheap part is one line beside the existing requireNonNull; the structural part (release on any Throwable, not only IOException) is a backlog row, not this commit.

findings.title: CommitLog.offsets()'s new javadoc states a concurrency reason the F1 fix removed, and the snapshot now runs ~K times more often than it is consumed
findings.failure_scenario: offsets() is new public surface in this commit and its javadoc says 'A COPY, not a view: the checkpoint writer reads this while commits continue, and handing out the live map would let it encode a half-applied delta'. After F1 the writer reads it on the commit thread, inside commitAll, so no commit is in flight and the copy defends against nothing -- the next reader of CommitLog is told an invariant the code no longer has, which is how the offsets()/nextSequence() race got introduced in the first place. The other half is measurable rather than stylistic: capture() runs on every commit, so each commit now does Map.copyOf over the whole offsets map plus a LinkedHashMap and a StreamOffsets per stream -- work proportional to every stream the chain has ever seen, discarded 999 times in 1000 at the shipped K. It replaces a per-commit cost of O(streams in this batch) with O(all streams), i.e. it puts commit-path allocation on the index x partition dimension. It is bounded by the batch rate rather than the record rate and sits next to a delta PUT that dominates it, so this is not a request-rate finding and probably not worth optimising; performance.md rule 8 wants the note either way, and the alternative that removes both the copy and the original race -- CommitLog publishing nextSequence volatile AFTER the offsets so a reader can only see the harmless skew -- deserves to be named as considered rather than left unmentioned.

answers.catch_throwable_in_observe: Broad but correct at this site: everything inside it is bookkeeping for records that are already durable and acknowledged, and letting it escape fails a whole BatchingSequencer window for writes that succeeded. It does not swallow silently -- WARNING with the throwable. Two caveats worth the commit body rather than a finding: a persistent failure inside capture() means dirty is never set and checkpoints stop entirely, so the cluster loses its recovery bound with only a per-commit log line to say so; and that log line is emitted once per delta with a stack trace, so the diagnostic itself scales with the commit rate. Logging without a metric is acceptable here -- observability.md was not selected for these paths, no metric is added anywhere in the diff, and F11 is recorded.
answers.closed_visibility: Sound. closed is volatile, so the plain write in close() is visible to the synchronized read in writeIfDirty and to the ticker's while (!closed) without the monitor. The residual race is inherent and benign: close() can land while writeIfDirty is already past the check and inside store.putIfAbsent, so one checkpoint PUT can complete after the fence -- it lands under the fenced epoch's own prefix, which the successor never reads and M4.8b1's key filter makes recovery skip.
answers.fence_path_close: No deadlock and no ordering problem. close() takes no monitor and does not join -- it sets closed and interrupts -- so the renewer never blocks behind a slow PUT, and a second close() from LocalSequencer.close() is an idempotent interrupt of a thread that is already stopping. One benign window remains, and it is the one the F6 comment describes from the other side: the renewer thread starts inside the LocalSequencer constructor, before sequencer.checkpoints is assigned, so a fence latched in that gap sees checkpoints == null and never closes the writer that is about to exist. It is harmless only by accident -- commitAll refuses once fenced, so observe() is never reached, dirty stays false and the orphaned ticker never PUTs -- and LocalSequencer.close() still reaps the thread.
answers.F10: Still M4.8c/M4.9's, not this commit's. M4/SPEC.md already owns it at lines 266 and 279 and assigns the discovery mechanism plus its ADR to M4.8; the growth of the ckpt/ prefix with uptime is stated there as a known consequence of nothing deleting checkpoints until M7. This commit's marginal effect on the existing recovery LIST is one extra key per K deltas against a prefix that already carries one key per delta -- a 1/K factor on a dimension that exists today, not a new dimension.
